segments.say: Let's turn to a halo that almost everyone notices, and almost everyone would rather not discuss. It's how attractive a person looks.

There's one more person in Felix's day. Her name is Imogen, and she's an intern, a few years younger than he is. She walked past his desk in the afternoon, striking and unhurried, and Felix, without being asked, had a quick thought. She's probably very good at this. He doesn't know a thing about her work. He's never seen a drawing of hers. But the thought arrived, fully formed.

He smiles a little at himself in the dark. It's not an unkind thought. It's even a generous one. But it's exactly the kind of thought that psychologists have studied for more than fifty years. When someone looks good to us, we tend to assume good things about them, even things that have nothing to do with looks. And the classic paper has a title like a proverb.

In 1972, three researchers, Karen Dion, Ellen Berscheid and Elaine Walster, published a paper in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology called, What is beautiful is good. It was a fairly small, careful experiment, and it asked a very direct question. If you look at photographs of people, do you assume that the better-looking ones are better people?

Here's the design. Sixty students, thirty men and thirty women, were told that the study was about accuracy in people perception. Each one was given three photographs of people of about the same age. One had been rated attractive by an earlier group of students, one average and one unattractive. They rated each person on twenty-seven personality traits. And then they predicted how happy each would be, and what jobs they might do.

show.what: Sixty students saw photographs of three people of similar age, one rated attractive, one average and one unattractive. They rated 27 personality traits and predicted each person's happiness and likely jobs.

segments.say: Imagine the room. A student at a table, with three photographs in front of them. No names. No stories. No voices. Nothing but three faces, and a form with twenty-seven traits to tick. And the task, which sounded perfectly reasonable, was to say what each person was probably like.

And here's the main result. The attractive person was given a higher average score on the positive personality traits, about sixty-five, compared with about fifty-six for the unattractive one, and about sixty-two for the average one. The more attractive the face, the better the character the students imagined.

show.title: Dion et al., 1972
show.label: average positive-personality score given to the attractive photo versus the unattractive photo (27 traits)

segments.say: It went beyond personality. Students expected the attractive people to have higher-status jobs. They expected them to have happier marriages, and to be happier overall. The better-looking the person in the photo, the better life the students predicted for them, in almost every area they were asked about.

It's a simple sentence, and it describes something that's very hard to unsee once you've noticed it. Not one of those students knew a thing about the people in the photographs. And yet, from a single image, they'd built lives, careers and marriages, and assigned them happiness in proportion to the way a face looked.

show.text: The better the face looked, the better the life imagined.

segments.say: There was one interesting exception in the results. When asked how good a parent each person would be, students didn't favour the attractive person. In fact, the average-looking person scored highest, and the attractive one a little lower. So the halo wasn't universal. It seemed to spread across some qualities, and stop at others.

That's a useful reminder. A halo isn't a blanket thrown over everything. It tends to follow the shape of a stereotype, spreading to the things that seem to fit the picture, like success and sociability, and skipping those that don't. It's a mind making a story that hangs together, and not a mind adding up scores.

Here's a quiet still-life. A bowl of apples on a wooden table, the shiniest one on top, catching the light. Without tasting any of them, you'd probably reach for that one. It looks the sweetest. It's a small, innocent kind of halo, and it's a good picture of how looks can promise more than they can deliver.

Decades later, other researchers asked a subtler question. Is it that attractive people get a boost, or that unattractive people get a penalty? A 2006 study by Griffin and Langlois, using photographs of young women, found the second to be more common. Unattractive faces were rated lower than medium ones on sociability, helpfulness and intelligence.

show.sub: Beauty is good, or ugly is bad?

segments.say: Here's the pattern. Unattractive faces were rated lowest on sociability, helpfulness and intelligence. But for helpfulness and intelligence, medium faces and attractive faces didn't differ. In other words, the penalty for being rated unattractive looked larger than the bonus for being rated attractive. The authors linked this to a tendency we have to weigh negative information more heavily.

show.title: What the 2006 study suggested
items: Unattractive faces were rated lowest on sociability
Also lowest on helpfulness and intelligence
Medium and attractive faces did not differ on helpfulness or intelligence
The penalty seemed bigger than the bonus

segments.say: Felix thinks about Imogen again. His quick thought, she's probably very good at this, wasn't mean. But it was borrowed from something else, her looks, and applied to something that had nothing to do with it. He doesn't know whether she's good at design. She might be brilliant. She might be learning, like him. And he's glad he noticed before he'd treated it as a fact.

He feels a little guilty for a second, and then he lets it go. The guilt isn't useful. These tendencies are old and automatic, and they show up in nearly everyone. What's useful is the noticing, and the willingness to wait and see her work. That's a perfectly good way of making amends with a stranger who didn't know she was being judged.

A fair caution applies here too. The 1972 study was small, with sixty students, and it's more than fifty years old. Attitudes, photographs and ideas of attractiveness have changed since. What has lasted is the general idea, that quick judgments of how someone looks can spill into judgments of who they are. The exact numbers matter less than the pattern.

And perhaps that's the gentlest way to put it. A face can promise things it has no way of delivering. A warm face can't guarantee warmth. A confident face can't guarantee skill. The promise is made by our own minds, and it's we who can choose whether to hold the other person to it.

show.text: A face can promise things it has no way of delivering.

segments.say: All of these studies have used faces, or words about people. But there's a different channel that carries a first impression, and it begins before we can even see someone. It's the sound of a single word.
A word that most of us say to a stranger within seconds, and the one that two researchers took apart on purpose.

Take a slow breath in, and let it go. Felix thinks of Imogen walking past, and of the borrowed thought that arrived with her. He lets it drift away, like a leaf on a slow stream. There's nothing to hold on to, and nothing to correct. There's only the dark, and the soft sound of his own breathing.
